newsitem.title: USA: Slow U.S. soy harvest stirs wheat seeding worries.
newsitem.headline: Slow U.S. soy harvest stirs wheat seeding worries.

text.p: This year's slow soybean harvest pace in the eastern Corn Belt has left some grain dealers and agronomists worried that farmers will be unable to plant their soft red winter wheat.
"There is a concern that they (farmers) won't be able to plant their wheat on time," said James Beuerlein, extension agronomist at Ohio State University.
Worries about delayed winter wheat crop planting boosted deferred soft red winter wheat contracts on the Chicago Board of Trade Wednesday, traders said.
SRW wheat for July, 1997 delivery closed 5-1/4 cents a bushel higher Wednesday at $3.77 a bushel and wheat for September, 1997 ended up 4-1/2 cents at $3.78.
Farmers were left skittish by last year's high incidence of crop failure and poor yield results, so some are scrapping plans to plant and have sold the seed, market observers said.
According to the latest USDA crop progress report for Ohio, a scant 12 percent of the winter wheat crop had been sown, compared with the five-year average of 34 percent.
"Farmers are beginning to wonder if they are going to get their wheat planted," one Ohio grain dealer said. "A few producers are selling the wheat (seed) that they intended to plant."
Bob Bischoff, seed production manager for Countrymark Cooperative in Indianapolis, Ind., said some central Ohio producers had attempted to return grain to the coop.
However, approximately 80 percent of Countrymark members' seed wheat in northern Ohio "was already in the ground," Bischoff said.

Because corn and soybean crops in Illinois were planted in a more timely manner, soft red wheat planting is proceeding more or less on schedule, said Emerson Nafziger, crop specialist with the Illinois extension service.
"In the southern part of the state this week the soybeans will be ready for harvest, and they (producers) will harvest as fast as they can," Nafziger said. "Then they'll put the wheat in quickly."

The latest crop progress data from the Illinois Agricultural Statistics Service showed that the soybean crop was 17 percent harvested in the week ended Sunday, behind the five-year average of 49 percent.
